## The program

```cpp
std::vector<int> values{};
int x{};
while (std::cin >> x) values.push_back(x);

std::cout << "size " << values.size() << "\n";

if (values.empty()) { /* three none lines */ }
else
{
    std::cout << "first " << values.front() << "\n";
    std::cout << "last " << values.back() << "\n";
    std::cout << "middle " << values[values.size() / 2] << "\n";
}
```

## When a vector earns its place

Every earlier exercise read a value, used it, and forgot it. That
is the cheapest thing a program can do and it works whenever the
answer is a running total, a count, or a maximum.

It stops working the moment an answer depends on *where* a value
was, or on comparing values to each other. "The middle one" cannot
be known until the last one has arrived. So the values have to be
kept, and since the count is unknown until the end, a fixed array
will not do either.

## push_back, and what it costs

`push_back` adds one element and grows the vector if there is no
room. Growing means allocating a bigger block and copying, which
sounds expensive and is not, because the capacity is **doubled**
rather than increased by one. Pushing n elements therefore costs
Ο(n) in total rather than Ο(n²) — each element is copied on
average a constant number of times.

If you do know the count in advance, `values.reserve(n)` avoids the
regrowth entirely. Here it is not known, so it cannot.

## Indexing an empty vector

This is the one that matters:

```cpp
std::vector<int> v{};
std::cout << v[0];          // undefined behaviour
std::cout << v.front();     // undefined behaviour
std::cout << v.at(0);       // throws std::out_of_range
```

`operator[]` does not check, by design: it is the fast one, and
making every access check would make vectors slower than arrays for
no benefit in correct code. It will often *appear* to work and print
whatever was in memory, which is worse than crashing.

`at()` checks and throws. Use it when the index came from outside
the program and you have not already validated it; use `[]` when
the loop bounds make the index safe by construction.

## front(), back(), and the - 1

`v.back()` and `v[v.size() - 1]` are the same element. The named
version says what it is for, and it cannot be written with the `- 1`
missing — which is the actual bug it prevents, since `v[v.size()]`
is one past the end and `size()` is unsigned so the mistake does not
even look like an off-by-one.

## What this does not check

Memory. Ten thousand `int`s is 40 KB and a vector will take as many
as the machine has; a program reading an unbounded stream into
memory is making a promise about the input size that this one can
make because the constraints say so.
